claims.normalized_claim: In Kyllo v. United States (2001) the Supreme Court held that where the Government uses a device that is not in general public use to explore details of the interior of a home that could not otherwise have been obtained without physical intrusion, the surveillance is a Fourth Amendment 'search' and is presumptively unreasonable without a warrant.
evidence_locations: Opinion of the Court (Scalia, J.), holding
counterevidence: Four justices (Stevens, dissenting) argued that measuring heat radiating from the home's exterior surface was not a search.
allowed_wording: The Court ruled that using a device not in general public use to learn what is inside a home is a search that normally needs a warrant.
prohibited_wording: The Court said police can never scan a home.

claims.normalized_claim: Kyllo v. United States was decided on June 11, 2001 by a 5-4 vote; the majority opinion was written by Justice Antonin Scalia (joined by Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer) and the dissent was written by Justice John Paul Stevens (joined by Chief Justice Rehnquist and Justices O'Connor and Kennedy).
allowed_wording: In a 5-4 decision in 2001, Justice Scalia wrote for the Court and Justice Stevens dissented.
claims.notes: Date/vote/author/lineup. The cross-ideological split (Scalia + Thomas + Ginsburg + Breyer + Souter vs. Rehnquist + O'Connor + Kennedy + Stevens) is accurate per the syllabus.

claims.normalized_claim: The majority reasoned that the Fourth Amendment draws a firm line at the entrance to the house that 'must be not only firm but also bright,' and tied its rule to whether the sense-enhancing technology used was 'not in general public use.'
evidence_locations: Opinion of the Court (Scalia, J.), 'firm but also bright' line and 'general public use' test
counterevidence: Critics note that what counts as 'general public use' is itself uncertain and shifts as technology spreads.
allowed_wording: The Court drew a firm, bright line at the entrance of the home, and its test turned on technology 'not in general public use.'
prohibited_wording: The Court said any use of technology near a home is illegal.
claims.notes: Doctrinal core plus the two exact quoted phrases from the opinion.

claims.normalized_claim: Justice Scalia's majority opinion grounded the ruling in the principle that 'at the very core' of the Fourth Amendment 'stands the right of a man to retreat into his own home and there be free from unreasonable governmental intrusion.'
evidence_locations: Opinion of the Court (Scalia, J.), 'core of the Fourth Amendment' passage (quoting Silverman v. United States)
allowed_wording: Scalia wrote that at the core of the Fourth Amendment is the right to retreat into your own home free from unreasonable intrusion.
claims.notes: Exact public-domain quote; the opinion itself quotes Silverman v. United States (1961).

claims.normalized_claim: On January 16, 1992, at about 3:20 a.m., federal agent William Elliott sat across the street from Danny Kyllo's home — one unit of a triplex on Rhododendron Drive in Florence, Oregon — and aimed an Agema Thermovision 210 thermal-imaging device at the house.
evidence_locations: Opinion of the Court (Scalia, J.), facts
allowed_wording: In January 1992 an agent scanned Kyllo's Oregon home from the street with an Agema Thermovision 210.
prohibited_wording: The device could see through the walls.
claims.notes: Real people by role; facts per the opinion. Danny Kyllo is a living person on the public record; handle factually.

claims.normalized_claim: The scan showed that the roof over the garage and a side wall of Kyllo's home were relatively hot compared with the rest of the house and with the neighboring units, and agent Elliott concluded that high-intensity (halide) lamps were being used to grow marijuana indoors.
evidence_locations: Opinion of the Court (Scalia, J.), facts
allowed_wording: The garage roof and a side wall read hotter than the rest, and the agent inferred grow lamps inside.
prohibited_wording: The scan proved a crime by itself.
claims.notes: Heat pattern and inference per opinion. Depict only heat/light, never drugs.

claims.normalized_claim: Together with an informant's tip and Kyllo's utility bills, the thermal scan helped obtain a warrant; the ensuing search found an indoor growing operation of more than 100 marijuana plants, and Kyllo was indicted on one count of manufacturing marijuana (21 U.S.C. 841(a)(1)) and entered a conditional guilty plea after his motion to suppress was denied.
evidence_locations: Opinion of the Court (Scalia, J.), facts and procedural posture
allowed_wording: The scan, a tip, and high power bills supported a warrant; the search found over 100 plants; Kyllo pleaded guilty conditionally after losing his suppression motion.
claims.notes: Procedural posture per opinion; conditional plea preserved the search question for appeal.

claims.normalized_claim: A thermal imager detects infrared radiation (heat) that virtually all objects emit but that is invisible to the naked eye, and converts it into an image based on relative warmth (black cool, white hot, gray between); it detects heat radiating from surfaces and does not physically see through walls.
evidence_locations: Opinion of the Court (Scalia, J.), description of thermal imagers
allowed_wording: A thermal imager reads invisible heat and turns it into a black-white-gray picture; it does not literally see through walls.
prohibited_wording: Thermal imaging is an X-ray that sees inside walls.
claims.notes: Technical description per the opinion; important so we do not overstate what the device does.

claims.normalized_claim: In dissent, Justice Stevens argued that the device measured only heat that had radiated off the home's exterior surface — 'off-the-wall' observation rather than 'through-the-wall' surveillance — and that heat which leaves a building enters the public domain, so the scan was not a search.
counterevidence: The majority rejected the distinction, holding the purpose and result were to learn the interior of the home without a warrant.
allowed_wording: Stevens dissented that the agent only read heat off the outside surface, which he called off-the-wall, not through-the-wall, surveillance.
prohibited_wording: All the justices agreed it was not a search.
claims.notes: Dissent for balance; the 'off-the-wall'/'through-the-wall' phrasing is Stevens' own.

claims.normalized_claim: The Court did not ban thermal imaging or automatically free Kyllo; it held that such a scan is a search requiring a warrant and remanded the case for the lower court to determine whether the warrant was supported by probable cause once the thermal-imaging evidence was set aside.
evidence_locations: Opinion of the Court (Scalia, J.), disposition / remand
allowed_wording: The ruling required a warrant and sent the case back to test the warrant without the thermal evidence; it did not outlaw thermal imaging.
prohibited_wording: Kyllo went free because of the ruling.
The Court made thermal imaging illegal.
claims.notes: Anti-overstatement claim: holding vs. outcome; the case was remanded, not simply reversed to acquittal.

claims.normalized_claim: Kyllo is widely treated as a landmark on how the Fourth Amendment applies to sense-enhancing technology and the home, and its 'not in general public use' standard is a moving line that courts return to as sensing devices such as drones and through-wall sensors become cheaper and more common.
evidence_locations: Oyez: significance / legacy of the general-public-use standard
counterevidence: Precisely because 'general public use' shifts as technology spreads, commentators disagree about how much protection the rule actually provides over time.
allowed_wording: Kyllo is the case courts keep returning to for surveillance technology and the home, and its 'general public use' line moves as devices spread.
prohibited_wording: Kyllo settled all questions about modern surveillance.
claims.notes: Legacy/interpretation kept neutral; B-grade context framed as ongoing debate, not settled fact.
